clue.text: The subject of his cutting may be brilliant

definitions.text: The subject of his cutting may be brilliant

parts.words: The subject of his cutting may be brilliant
parts.note: a gem-cutter works on stones, and a diamond cut in a particular way is called a brilliant, so the person is identified by his craft

explanation.surface: Someone's cutting remarks, aimed at a subject, may come out witty and dazzling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brilliant' reads as praise for a sharp wit, but it is the name of a diamond cut with many facets.
explanation.definitionFit: A gem-cutter or engraver of precious stones is the craftsman meant, and his finished diamond may be a brilliant.

clue.text: Plaguy flier

parts.note: an insect that swarms in plagues, the eighth plague of Egypt in the Bible

explanation.surface: An annoying pilot.
explanation.definitionFit: This grasshopper-like insect flies in vast swarms that devastate crops, as in the biblical plagues.

clue.text: She had a dour attachment to show

parts.note: pomp is ceremonial show or display
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman had a grim attachment to showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is the definition: Madame de Pompadour, mistress of Louis XV. 'Had ... attachment to' joins A DOUR to POMP.
explanation.definitionFit: Madame de Pompadour was the famous mistress of the French king Louis XV, a celebrated woman.

clue.text: A physician has something to prescribe

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
aught is an old word for anything or something

explanation.surface: A doctor has a remedy to give a patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To prescribe' stands for a thing to prescribe: a draught is a dose of liquid medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: A dose of liquid medicine is the sort of remedy a doctor orders for a patient.

clue.text: What cooks do with books

parts.note: the two words cooks and books share their final sound, so the question is about the words rather than kitchens

explanation.surface: How chefs use their recipe books.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a question about cookery books, but it is about the two words: they end with the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Words with matching end sounds correspond in verse, as cooks and books do.

clue.text: Play the nark in one of 18

parts.note: 18 across is FORMS, school classes, so one of them is a single class

explanation.surface: A pupil acts the sneak within one of the school classes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One of 18' sends you to 18 across (classes) for a single class. A nark is British slang for a police informer, so to play the nark is to tell tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A nark passes secrets to the authorities, so playing that part means telling on someone.

clue.text: Dr. Jekyll underwent this, as well as physical, change

definitions.text: Dr. Jekyll underwent this, as well as physical, change

parts.words: Dr. Jekyll underwent this, as well as physical, change
parts.note: Jekyll turned into Hyde, changing his body and also his name

explanation.surface: Dr Jekyll's transformation was more than just bodily.
explanation.walkthrough: In Stevenson's story Dr Jekyll becomes Mr Hyde, so besides changing shape he changes what he is called.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to a name, and Jekyll took a new name.

clue.text: Extravagant change of route

indicators.note: a change of the word route means its letters are altered in order

explanation.surface: An excessive diversion from the usual way.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bizarre or beyond the bounds of convention is extravagant.

clue.text: Fools on the increase, we hear, in the fens

indicators.note: we hear signals that the phrase is to be said out loud and matched by sound

parts.note: a growing number of fools means more asses, an ass being a fool

explanation.surface: Idiots multiplying out in the marshy country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More asses' (fools on the increase) is said out loud to give the word for bogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Fens are marshy wetlands, so they are bogs or swamps.

clue.text: Overture to The Ring

parts.note: not Wagner's opera cycle but an offer of marriage that leads to an engagement ring

explanation.surface: The prelude to Wagner's operatic cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Ring' and 'Overture' suggest Wagner, but an overture is also an approach or offer, here one that leads to an engagement ring.
explanation.definitionFit: An offer of marriage is the opening move before the engagement ring.

clue.text: Business organizer, avoiding third-party risks ?

parts.note: a person who floats firms, read whimsically as one who encourages pairs, since two's company and three's a crowd, so a third party is avoided

explanation.surface: A business founder steers clear of insurance claims from outsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Third-party risks' suggests insurance, but the joke is the saying 'two's company, three's a crowd': someone who promotes company keeps a third person out.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who sets up and floats new firms is a business organizer by profession.

clue.text: Get our measure with a leg-break-that's bright

parts.note: a span is a measure of length, the stretch of a spread hand

indicators.note: to break the word leg is to scramble its letters

explanation.surface: A cricketer gauges the field and bowls a leg-break that dazzles.
explanation.walkthrough: A leg-break is a cricket delivery spinning from the leg side; here 'break' tells you to rearrange LEG into GLE. 'Get our' is linking padding.
explanation.definitionFit: A small shiny disc sewn on clothes is something that glitters and catches the light.

clue.text: Boatmen getting a kick, out of their wagers?

definitions.meaning: people who propel flat-bottomed boats with a pole on a river

definitions.text: getting a kick, out of their wagers?
definitions.meaning: people who punt kick a ball, and the same word means gamblers who place bets

explanation.surface: Boatmen enjoy a thrill from their bets.
explanation.walkthrough: To punt is to pole a boat, to kick a ball dropped from the hands, and in British usage to place a bet, so the word works three ways.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names those who pole a river boat and also those who bet, who may also kick a ball.

clue.text: Must be hard to overcome this

definitions.text: Must be hard to overcome this

parts.words: Must be hard to overcome this
parts.note: the opposite quality to hardness can only be beaten by being hard, read as a literal statement rather than a remark on difficulty

explanation.surface: Some obstacle must be a tough thing to get past.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as 'this must be difficult to overcome', but it means the opposite of hard is what hardness defeats.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of being yielding or gentle is the opposite of hardness, so only hardness overcomes it.

clue.text: Common, but maybe not on Sunday

definitions.text: Common, but maybe not on Sunday

parts.words: Common, but maybe not on Sunday
parts.note: ordinary or routine, yet read literally as happening on all seven days, which a Sunday rest might break

explanation.surface: Something ordinary that is perhaps avoided on the Sabbath.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means commonplace, but taken literally it means happening daily, which a Sunday off would spoil.
explanation.definitionFit: Something routine and ordinary is commonplace, happening all the time.

clue.text: Cruel difficult, making money

indicators.note: difficult here describes the letters as awkward, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A harsh and hard person earns a living.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is a scornful word for money, as in filthy profit.

clue.text: So cereals can be' cooked herein

definitions.text: So cereals can be' cooked herein

indicators.note: cooked signals that the letters given are to be mixed up

explanation.surface: Grains may be cooked in this dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep lidded dish for slow-cooking food in the oven is one in which grains could be cooked.

clue.text: Twig what the missing marksman is?

definitions.meaning: a twig is a small shoot growing from a branch
a marksman who misses is off with his shot, read as two words

explanation.surface: Understand what the gunman who missed is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twig' looks like the British slang verb 'understand', but it is a noun, a small branch.
explanation.definitionFit: A twig is a side growth from a plant, and a marksman who misses is off in his shooting.

clue.text: Classes for writing

definitions.meaning: school year groups in British schools are called by this word
printed documents to be filled in by hand

explanation.surface: School classes spent on writing practice.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both groups of pupils in a British school and printed papers with blanks to fill in.

clue.text: He gets in, and leaps about backwards, the dog!

indicators.note: backwards signals reading the whole assembly from right to left
about means surrounding, so the word leaps is placed around in

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dog bounds in, jumping around, then reverses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts LEAPS around IN to give LEINAPS; 'backwards' reverses all of it. 'He gets' is linking padding.
explanation.definitionFit: A spaniel is a breed of dog with long drooping ears.

clue.text: Lauder to get us oil per laps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters given might be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: Praise for a singer, offered to get some oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lauder' looks like Harry Lauder the Scottish music-hall singer, but it is one who lauds, a praiser.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lauds is a praiser, one who delivers a speech of praise.

clue.text: Well might be one of these effusive types

definitions.text: Well might be one of these
definitions.meaning: an oil well that spouts freely is called by this name
people who talk with excessive enthusiasm

explanation.surface: Gushing people may well be among these.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' reads as an adverb but is a noun, an oil well.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both oil wells that spout and people who enthuse too much.

clue.text: Sources of wild laughter

parts.note: animals of the African wild known for their laughing call, rather than causes of hysterical mirth

explanation.surface: Things that set off uncontrollable giggling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild laughter' suggests hysterics, but it is laughter from animals in the wild.
explanation.definitionFit: These African scavengers make a call that sounds like human laughter.

clue.text: Abstract the total, Miss Morison

parts.note: a total is a sum, the result of adding up
Mary Morison is the woman addressed in a song by Robert Burns

explanation.surface: Give a précis of the totals, Miss Morison, says the boss to a secretary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abstract' is a noun here, a brief outline. Mary Morison is the subject of a Robert Burns poem.
explanation.definitionFit: An abstract is a short outline of a document's main points.

clue.text: After a little while tea becomes coffee

indicators.note: After places the second piece behind the first in the answer

parts.note: mo is short for moment, a little while
cha is a slang word for tea

explanation.surface: After a moment, the tea turns into coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: MO (a moment, British informal) comes first; 'After' puts CHA behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocha is a fine Arabian coffee, named after a Yemeni port.

clue.text: The end of Edwin Drood's remains one

definitions.text: The end of Edwin Drood's remains one

parts.words: The end of Edwin Drood's remains one
parts.note: Dickens died before finishing his last novel about Edwin Drood, so how its story ends is still unsolved, and its title starts with the same word

explanation.surface: Drood's corpse is found in the final chapter of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains' looks like a body, but it means 'stays'. Dickens left The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished, so its ending is still unknown.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unexplained or unknown, like the unwritten conclusion of Dickens's last novel, is an enigma.

clue.text: A mix-up with myself and the general

parts.note: me is the speaker referring to himself
Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general in the American Civil War

explanation.surface: A confusion involving me and the commanding officer.
explanation.walkthrough: General Lee, the Confederate commander, is a stock crossword general.
explanation.definitionFit: A confused scuffle or brawl is a jumbled mix-up of people.

clue.text: Very rarely it makes union loan become possible

indicators.note: possible implies the letters could become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Getting a loan for a trade union approved happens hardly ever.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means almost never, as a second full moon in a month is rare.

clue.text: Following them, you may leave then behind

definitions.text: Following them, you may leave then behind

parts.words: Following them, you may leave then behind
parts.note: when you track paths or tracks, you also make tracks of your own that stay behind you

explanation.surface: Walking after a group of people, you may outpace them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave them behind' suggests overtaking, but walking a path also leaves a track behind you.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracks or footpaths are what you follow and also what you leave as you go.

clue.text: They have no consideration for their betters

definitions.text: They have no consideration for their betters

parts.words: They have no consideration for their betters
parts.note: a bookmaker who refuses to pay winning bets gives no payment to the people who bet with him, consideration meaning payment

explanation.surface: Snobs who show no respect for their superiors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Betters' looks like social superiors but means people who place bets; 'consideration' is a payment rather than courtesy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bookmakers who run off without paying winning punters give their bettors nothing.
